claims.text: PasswordHasher.Hash generates a 16-byte random salt via RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes, then Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2 with 100_000 iterations, SHA256, and a 32-byte output; returns "{iterations}.{salt base64}.{hash base64}".

PasswordHasher.Verify splits the stored string on '.', parses iterations/salt/hash, recomputes Pbkdf2 with the same salt and iteration count, and compares the result to the stored hash via CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals.
AuthController.Login is the only call site of PasswordHasher.Verify in this app's code; PasswordHasher.Hash has no call site at all - no registration endpoint exists yet.

claims.text: Migration AddPasswordHashToCustomers adds a nullable text column password_hash to customers, then backfills one literal hash string for customer ids 1-5 via a raw SQL UPDATE, not five separate Hash calls.
System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes returns a new cryptographically random byte sequence on every call, so two calls never return the same bytes in practice.
CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals compares two byte spans in an amount of time that does not depend on where the first differing byte is, specifically to resist timing attacks.
PBKDF2 (Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2) is a one-way key derivation function: there is no computationally feasible way to recover the original password from its output alone.
claims.source_hint: .NET API docs, Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2, and PBKDF2's definition as a one-way KDF (RFC 8018 / NIST SP 800-132)
